results.corrected_extracted: Primary source of the review's Saturday-night figures, read in full. Three groups of 15 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30, recruited by word of mouth among people who regularly went to one large nightclub in north-east London: a regular group with ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, a novice group with one to nine, and a comparison group who had never taken it. Each person noted on a questionnaire the drugs taken that night: the regular group 1.80 tablets on average and the novice group 1.45, which the authors call slightly more; the comparison group took none. No spread, range or test of the difference is printed, no testing of the tablets is reported, and the paper does not discuss tolerance. Other drugs that night (comparison, novice, regular): alcohol 10, 5 and 6 people, cannabis 3, 1 and 2, cocaine 2, 2 and 4, amphetamine 1 novice. Editors' check against Parrott (2005), p. 74: the review gives 1.45 and 1.80 correctly and calls the record prospective (here a self-report on the night), but describes the regular group as more than 10 occasions, where this paper's Methods say ten or more.
results.note: Numbers match. 'The tablets were not tested' says more than the paper: it records drugs by self-report and mentions no testing. Parrott (2005) not checked (single source); this paper's Discussion (pp. 266-267) also says more than ten occasions.

results.corrected_extracted: Field study with no placebo and no random allocation: unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30 (regular, novice, comparison: group means 21.4, 22.8 and 21.3 years; women/men 8/7, 8/7 and 10/5), recruited by word of mouth among friends and acquaintances who regularly went to one large nightclub in north-east London, in three groups of 15: ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, one to nine, and never. Each rated 16 moods on 0 to 100 lines on a hand-held computer at a drug-free session at their own or the experimenter's home before the night out (no MDMA for at least 1 week and no other illicit drug for over 24 hours, by their own account), at the club 2 to 8 hours after taking their tablets (8 of the 30 at 8 to 16 hours; the comparison group at equivalent times), and 2 and 7 days later. Drugs taken that night were self-noted on a questionnaire; no testing of the tablets is reported. In the comparison group 10 of 15 drank alcohol (5.0 drinks per drinker), 3 smoked cannabis and 2 took cocaine; in the novice and regular groups 5 and 6 drank (2.7 and 3.7 drinks), 1 and 2 smoked cannabis, 2 and 4 took cocaine, and 1 novice took amphetamine. The aims of the study were described to each person beforehand; the study was approved by the University Ethics Committee.
results.corrected_locator: Materials and methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 262); Assessment measures, 3rd paragraph (p. 262); Procedures and ethics, 1st paragraph (pp. 262-263) and 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 263)
results.note: All numbers match. Baseline was at the subject's or experimenter's home; the paper reports no tablet testing but does not say none occurred; age/gender order (regular, novice, comparison) made explicit; the 2-8 h detail is on p. 263.

results.corrected_extracted: Means only, no spread, with Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group at each session (comparison, novice, regular). At the club: good tempered 85, 90 and 88, no difference; sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); the comparison group less sober (46 against 78, p < 0.05, and 67) and less steady (50 against 76, p < 0.05, and 71, p < 0.10). Two days later: sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); energetic 72, 62 and 56 (regular p < 0.05). Seven days later none of these differed (sad 22, 25 and 21; depressed 37, 37 and 39; unsociable 22, 18 and 18; good tempered 86, 84 and 87); both ecstasy groups were less drowsy than the comparison group (28, p < 0.05, and 25, p < 0.01, against 38). Before the night the novice group was already sadder than the comparison group (31 against 22, p < 0.05). Group by session interactions in two-way analyses of variance: p < 0.001 for abnormal, depressed and sad; p < 0.01 for sober, unpleasant and unsociable; p < 0.05 for good tempered and steady; not significant for the other eight scales; no F values or degrees of freedom printed.
results.note: Every mean, p-level and Table 1 interaction checked on the image: all match. Only change: two comparisons (baseline sadness, day-7 drowsiness) now name the comparison group, as Table 2's footnote does.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors call the absence of better moods in the ecstasy groups than in the comparison group on the night unexpected and give four possible reasons: earlier studies mostly had no comparison group of other clubbers, who would also be expected to feel good on their Saturday night out; the comparison group had taken other drugs, mainly alcohol, and a drug-free group is needed in future studies; ratings such as good tempered were already near the top of the scale in the comparison group; and the scales had no items on elation or empathy. They describe a range of negative moods two days later and marked swings over the week in depression, sadness, calmness, pleasantness and sociability in the ecstasy groups against fairly stable levels in the comparison group, attribute the low moods to serotonin depletion, which was not measured, and conclude that the good moods of all the clubbers show the importance of context and expectancy.
results.note: Location right. Fixes: the paper says clubbers 'would be expected to experience good feelings', not that they expect a good night; the ceiling was 'in the control group'; 'better moods' now names its comparison; stability covered five named feelings only.
